questions.question: In Lab 9, what does `npm init -y` do?
options: Downloads React from the internet
Creates a `package.json` file listing the project's scripts and dependencies
Starts the Vite development server
Creates the `src` folder and an `App.jsx` file
questions.explanation: `npm init -y` creates `package.json`. The `npm install` commands are what download libraries like Vite and React, and `npm run dev` starts the server.

questions.question: After you add `"dev": "vite dev"` to the `scripts` section of `package.json`, what happens when you run `npm run dev`?
options: The app is built into static files for deployment
All of your dependencies are installed
Your tests are run
A local development server starts, with hot reload and bundling enabled
questions.explanation: Adding the script means `npm run dev` runs `vite dev`, which serves your app locally. With hot reload, the browser updates when you save a file.

questions.question: What does `main.jsx` do in this lab?
options: It finds the `<div id="app">` in the HTML and renders the `App` component into it
It defines the `Profile` component
It stores the list of people
It installs React and ReactDOM
questions.explanation: `createRoot(document.getElementById("app"))` creates a React root inside the div, and `root.render(<App />)` injects the `App` component there. `index.html` loads `main.jsx` with a `<script>` tag.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `<>...</>` in `App.jsx`?
options: It marks a comment in JSX
It imports a component from another file
It's a React Fragment: it lets you return multiple elements without adding an extra wrapper `<div>` to the page
It turns the elements inside into a list
questions.explanation: A component has to return a single parent element. A fragment groups siblings together without adding anything to the DOM.

questions.question: You created `Profile.jsx` with `export default function Profile() { ... }`. What do you need in `App.jsx` before you can write `<Profile />`?
options: `import { Profile } from "./Profile.jsx";`
`require("Profile");`
`import Profile from "./Profile.jsx";`
Nothing, because React finds components automatically
questions.explanation: A default export is imported without braces, using the path to the file. Without the import, `Profile` isn't defined in `App.jsx`.

questions.question:
Given this tag, how should `Profile.jsx` receive and display the name?

```jsx
<Profile name="Anita" />
```
questions.explanation: React passes all of a tag's attributes in a single `props` object. `{ name }` in the parameter list *destructures* it to pull out `name`, and `{name}` in the JSX displays the value. Without braces, `name` would be displayed as the literal text "name". Without the destructuring, `name` is undefined (or is the whole props object).

questions.question:
What does `

{name}

` display, compared to `

name

`?
options: Both display the value of the `name` variable
The first displays the literal word "name", and the second displays the value
The first causes an error, and the second displays the value
The first displays the value of the `name` variable (such as "Anita"), and the second displays the literal word "name"
questions.explanation: In JSX, curly braces switch from markup to a JavaScript expression. Anything outside the braces is plain text.

questions.question: Which JSX attribute is used to give an element a CSS class?
options: `class`
`className`
`cssClass`
`style-class`
questions.explanation: In JSX, you write `className="profile"` because `class` is already a reserved word in JavaScript. The lab's `Profile` component uses `<section className="profile">`.

The original `people` array, changed to hold components
Nothing, because `map` only works on numbers
A new array of 4 `Profile` components, one for each person
questions.explanation: `map` runs the function once per item and returns a new array of the results. React renders each component in the array. The original `people` array isn't changed.

questions.question: Which `onClick` is correct for calling `addOne` when a button is clicked?
options: `<button onClick={addOne}>`
`<button onClick={addOne()}>`
`<button onClick="addOne">`
`<button onClick=addOne>`
questions.explanation: In JSX you pass the function itself in curly braces, with no parentheses, and React calls it when the click happens. With `addOne()`, the function would be called during rendering instead of waiting for the click.

questions.question:
What does this line do?

```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```
options: It creates two separate state variables, `count` and `setCount`, both starting at 0
It creates a state variable `count` that starts at 0, and a function `setCount` that changes it and redraws the component
It sets `count` to 0 every time the component redraws
It makes `count` a constant that can't change
questions.explanation: `useState(0)` returns an array with the current value and a setter function. The square brackets are array destructuring that picks out both. Calling the setter updates the value and redraws the component.

questions.question: Why does the lab use `setCount(count + 1)` instead of just `count = count + 1` (or `count++`)?
options: `setCount` is faster than the `=` operator
JavaScript doesn't allow adding to numbers without a function
Only the setter function updates the state *and* triggers a redraw of the component
The `=` operator works but makes the code harder to read
questions.explanation: React doesn't watch regular variables. Calling the setter from `useState` tells React the state changed so it can redraw. (Since `count` is declared with `const`, reassigning it would throw an error anyway.)

questions.question: You add six `<ButtonCount />` tags to `App.jsx`, then click the third button 5 times. What do the buttons show?
options: Only the third button shows 5. Each component has its own independent state
All six buttons show 5
The third button and every button after it show 5
Every button shows 1, because only the latest click counts
questions.explanation: Each `<ButtonCount />` is a separate instance of the component, and each one has its own `useState`. Clicking one doesn't change the others.
